title: Dose, half life and duration of activity

segs.text: Module seven B, objective two. How dose and half life change the duration of the response. The duration of activity, t eff, is how long a single I V bolus keeps the plasma level at or above C eff, the minimum effective concentration, also called the M E C. Every one of her problems is a one compartment open model with first order elimination, so after the bolus the level falls by the same fraction each hour. C zero is the level just after the bolus, the dose D zero divided by the volume of distribution, V D.

card.m: t<sub>eff</sub>: time the level stays at or above C<sub>eff</sub> after one IV bolus
one compartment, first order: the same fraction lost each hour

segs.text: With first order elimination the level halves every half life. So t eff is the number of halvings from C zero down to C eff, times the half life. Doubling the dose doubles C zero, and a level twice as high needs exactly one more halving to reach the same C eff. So each doubling of the dose adds one half life to t eff; it does not double t eff, and four times the dose adds two half lives. She wrote, each time we double the dose, we'll get an additional half life. A larger V D gives a lower C zero, and a higher C eff leaves fewer halvings, so either one shortens t eff.

card.m: t<sub>eff</sub> = number of halvings from C<sub>0</sub> to C<sub>eff</sub> × t<sub>½</sub>
V<sub>D</sub> larger or C<sub>eff</sub> higher → t<sub>eff</sub> shorter

segs.text: The half life sets the length of each halving. Doubling the half life at the same dose keeps the same number of halvings, each twice as long, so t eff doubles. Liver or kidney disease that lowers elimination prolongs the half life, so the drug is retained longer, and both the duration of activity and the possibility of toxicity increase. The dose works differently: plotted against dose, t eff rises steeply at low doses and then flattens, because each added milligram adds less duration, and it takes a doubling of the dose to add one more half life.

card.m: e.g. textbook table: 2 × t<sub>½</sub>: 3.24 → 6.48 hr; 2 × dose: 3.24 → 3.98 hr
liver or kidney disease → t<sub>½</sub> longer → t<sub>eff</sub> longer, toxicity risk higher
t<sub>eff</sub> against dose: steep, then flat; each doubling adds one t<sub>½</sub>

segs.text: t eff is when the I V bolus line, C zero e to the minus k t, reaches C eff. In natural logs, t eff is the natural log of C zero over C eff, divided by k. With the half life, t eff is one point four four, one over zero point six nine three, times t half times the natural log of D zero over V D times C eff. The dose is inside the log, so doubling it adds the natural log of two over k, one half life, while the half life multiplies everything, so t eff is in proportion to it. The base ten form gives slightly less than the natural log form, because its two point three rounds two point three zero three.

card.m: t<sub>eff</sub> = {{frac:2.3(log C<sub>0</sub> − log C<sub>eff</sub>)|k}}: 26.32 hr against 26.35 hr

segs.text: Her review poll: a one gram I V bolus, a V D of twelve point five liters, a half life of four hours and an M E C of twenty milligrams per liter. C zero is eighty milligrams per liter, which halves to forty and then to twenty, two halvings, so t eff is eight hours, her key. With five hundred milligrams, C zero is forty milligrams per liter, one halving, four hours, her key. Halving the dose halved the duration only because forty is exactly twice the M E C. A two gram dose, which she did not ask, would start at one hundred sixty milligrams per liter, three halvings, twelve hours, not sixteen, so doubling the dose does not double t eff, as her poll key says.

card.m: D<sub>0</sub> = 1000 mg, V<sub>D</sub> = 12.5 L, t<sub>½</sub> = 4 hr, MEC = 20 mg/L
40 mg/L = 2 × MEC: the 500 mg t<sub>eff</sub> is exactly 1 t<sub>½</sub>
e.g. 2 g: C<sub>0</sub> = 160 mg/L, 3 halvings = 12 hr, not 16

segs.text: Her slide practice problem gives an antibiotic an M E C of zero point two micrograms per milliliter, the same number in milligrams per liter, a V D of twenty four liters and a k of zero point one five per hour. For a two hundred fifty milligram dose, k is given, so the natural log form is quickest. C zero is ten point four two milligrams per liter, about fifty two times the M E C, and t eff is twenty six point three five hours. Five hundred milligrams gives thirty point nine seven hours, four point six two hours more, which is one half life, and one thousand milligrams adds a second half life, to about thirty five point six hours.

card.m: MEC 0.2 mcg/mL = 0.2 mg/L; V<sub>D</sub> 24 L; k 0.15 hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: Her follow up on the slide problem asks the dose that doubles t eff, from twenty six point three five to fifty two point seven hours. Solved for the dose, D zero equals C eff times V D times e to the plus k t eff. The exponent is positive because the dose must be larger than C eff times V D, four point eight milligrams, the amount that would give exactly the M E C at the start. The target time is in the exponent, so each added half life of duration doubles the dose. The answer is about thirteen grams, fifty two times the two hundred fifty milligram dose, for twice the duration; doubling the half life at two hundred fifty milligrams would also double t eff.

Her practice three uses the half life form: a twenty milligram per kilogram I V bolus, a V D of zero point three liters per kilogram, a half life of three point six hours and an M E C of seven point two milligrams per liter. The kilograms cancel, so C zero is sixty six point six seven milligrams per liter, and t eff is eleven point five six hours. The doubled dose gives fifteen point one six hours, three point six hours more, one half life.

card.m: 20 mg/kg, V<sub>D</sub> 0.3 L/kg, t<sub>½</sub> 3.6 hr, MEC 7.2 mcg/mL = 7.2 mg/L
2 × dose: C0 = 133.3 mg/L → 15.16 hr, + 3.6 hr = 1 t½

segs.text: Her poll asked, true or false, whether doubling the I V bolus dose of a linear, first order drug gives a two fold increase in the duration of activity, and her key is false. On her quiz, doubling the dose adds one half life to the duration; it doubles neither the duration nor the half life. C zero does double with the dose, but because the dose is inside the log, the duration rises by only one half life. Other wrong answers she sees: changing the number when converting the M E C from micrograms per milliliter to milligrams per liter, e to the minus k t instead of e to the plus k t in the dose equation, and a base ten log in the natural log form.

card.m: wrong: MEC number changed; e<sup>−kt</sup> in the D<sub>0</sub> line; log in the ln form
